title: First voyage of Christopher Columbus
summary: On 12 October 1492, Christopher Columbus's expedition made landfall on the Lucayan Taíno island of Guanahaní after sailing from Palos, Spain. The transatlantic voyage initiated sustained European contact with the Americas, leading to rapid colonisation, enslavement, and devastating Indigenous demographic collapse.
card: Financed by Queen Isabella and King Ferdinand of Castile and Aragon, Christopher Columbus led three ships across the Atlantic Ocean, departing Palos in August 1492 and sighting the Bahamian island of Guanahaní in October. The voyagers met Lucayan Taíno islanders, abducted several captives to serve as interpreters, and explored northern Cuba and Hispaniola before the flagship Santa María wrecked on Christmas Day. Leaving thirty-nine crewmen at the makeshift outpost of La Navidad, Columbus returned to Europe in March 1493, unleashing centuries of Spanish imperial conquest, forced labor regimes, and devastating epidemic mortality across the Caribbean.
what:
On 3 August 1492, Genoese mariner Christopher Columbus departed Palos de la Frontera, Andalusia, commanding three vessels—the flagship nao Santa María and caravels Pinta and Niña—chartered under the authority of the Catholic Monarchs of Castile and Aragon. The expedition paused in the Canary Islands for provisioning and repairs, setting out westward from San Sebastián de La Gomera on 6 September into the open ocean. Following thirty-three days of westward navigation, lookouts aboard the Pinta sighted land at 2:00 a.m. on 12 October 1492 (Julian calendar; 21 October proleptic Gregorian). Columbus landed later that morning on an island in the Lucayan archipelago called Guanahaní by its inhabitants, claiming it for the Crown of Castile and naming it San Salvador.

On the beach, the Spaniards encountered Lucayan people, northern relatives of the Greater Antillean Taíno. Columbus recorded their generosity, physical beauty, body paint, and lack of iron weaponry, while noting their potential as servants and converts; he detained six Indigenous islanders to carry back to Spain as interpreters. Over the following eleven weeks, guided by kidnapped captives, Columbus navigated south and west through the Bahamas, landing on northeastern Cuba on 28 October and northern Hispaniola on 6 December.

Disaster struck on the night of 24–25 December 1492 when the Santa María ran aground on a coral reef off northern Hispaniola. Aided by the Taíno cacique Guacanagaríx, the crew salvaged its timbers to build a fortified garrison named La Navidad. Columbus left thirty-nine men to garrison the fort and gather gold, departing aboard the Niña on 4 January 1493. After surviving severe winter storms that forced temporary stops in the Azores and Lisbon, Columbus anchored at Palos on 15 March 1493.

The geographical identity of Guanahaní remains debated among scholars, with San Salvador (formerly Watling Island) remaining the leading candidate alongside Samana Cay and the Plana Cays.

uncertainty.note: Exact calendar dates recorded in the ship log: departure from Palos on 3 August 1492 and return on 15 March 1493 in the Julian calendar (12 August 1492 and 24 March 1493 in the proleptic Gregorian calendar). Landfall at Guanahaní took place on 12 October 1492 Julian (21 October 1492 Gregorian).

how:
The voyage was spurred by European mercantile competition to secure direct access to South and East Asian maritime trade after the Ottoman conquest of Constantinople (1453) blocked overland Silk Road routes and Portugal monopolized the African coastal passage. Following the completion of the Reconquista at Granada in January 1492, King Ferdinand and Queen Isabella approved Columbus's enterprise under the Capitulations of Santa Fe, promising him hereditary knighthood, the office of Admiral of the Ocean Sea, the viceroyalty of newly acquired territories, and ten percent of all trade revenues.

Columbus assembled three ships at Palos de la Frontera: the flagship nao Santa María and the caravels Pinta and Niña, manned by Spanish sailors. The fleet sailed south to the Canary Islands, taking advantage of trade winds and the North Equatorial Current to cross the Atlantic westward at roughly twenty-four to twenty-eight degrees north latitude. Utilizing dead reckoning and compass navigation, Columbus tracked distance while recording a false lower daily progress in his public journal to reassure his anxious crew.

After encountering migrating birds and carved vegetation indicating land, lookouts sighted Guanahaní on 12 October. Guided by captured Indigenous pilots, Columbus navigated through the Bahamas, explored northern Cuba, and proceeded to Hispaniola. The grounding of the Santa María on a reef off Cap-Haïtien on Christmas Eve compelled Columbus to construct the fort of La Navidad using salvaged timbers, leaving thirty-nine crewmen behind. Sailing eastward aboard the Niña, Columbus steered northward into higher latitudes to catch prevailing westerly winds across the stormy North Atlantic, reaching the Azores, Lisbon, and finally Palos in March 1493.
why_it_matters:
Columbus's first voyage permanently united the Eastern and Western Hemispheres, initiating the Columbian Exchange: a global, reciprocal transfer of plants, animals, cultures, and human populations that reshaped world agriculture and ecology. European crops and domestic livestock transformed American landscapes, while American maize, potatoes, cassava, and sweet potatoes supported rapid demographic growth across Eurasia and Africa.

For Indigenous Americans, however, European landfall triggered catastrophe. Spanish colonial extraction began almost immediately with the forced encomienda system in gold mines and plantations. Deprived of immunity to Old World infectious pathogens such as smallpox, measles, and influenza, and subjected to brutal labor and warfare, the Taíno population of Hispaniola declined precipitously: traditional historical estimates recorded that native numbers collapsed from roughly one million to thirty thousand within two decades. While recent genomic analyses suggest smaller pre-contact baseline populations, they confirm catastrophic demographic collapse across the islands. This rapid destruction of Indigenous Caribbean labor prompted Spanish administrators to begin importing enslaved Africans as early as 1502, establishing the foundations of the transatlantic slave trade and plantation slavery in the Americas.

If Columbus had perished at sea or failed to secure royal backing in 1492, transatlantic contact would still have occurred within years, as illustrated by Pedro Álvares Cabral's voyage reaching Brazil in 1500; however, an alternate landfall would have established different colonial boundaries, legal institutions, and initial European alliances across the Americas.

related.because: Spanish colonisation and rapid Indigenous demographic collapse in the Caribbean after 1492 drove European colonists to import enslaved African laborers from 1502 onward.
The Caribbean outposts founded following Columbus's first voyage served as the administrative and military launching points for the Spanish expedition against the Aztec Empire.

The fleet refits in the Canary Islands, departing La Gomera on 6 September 1492 Julian westward into the uncharted Atlantic.
Following thirty-three days of westward ocean sailing, lookouts aboard the Pinta sight land at 2:00 a.m. on 12 October 1492 Julian.
Columbus makes landfall on Guanahaní, claiming it as San Salvador and abducting several Lucayan Taíno to serve as guides.
Exploring Cuba and Hispaniola, the flagship Santa María runs aground on Christmas Eve; its timbers form the outpost of La Navidad.
Columbus returns to Palos in March 1493; within two decades, forced labor and European diseases devastate the Indigenous Caribbean population.

perspectives.holder: Samuel Eliot Morison, the Bahamian Government, and the Gerace Research Centre (San Salvador / Watling Island hypothesis)
perspectives.account: Watling Island (renamed San Salvador in 1926) matches Columbus's description of a large interior lagoon, barrier reefs, and coastal morphology, representing the traditional consensus landfall site of Guanahaní.

perspectives.holder: Joseph Judge, National Geographic Society (1986), and Augustus V. Fox (Samana Cay hypothesis)
perspectives.account: Computer modeling of transatlantic winds, currents, and dead-reckoning courses places Columbus's landfall at Samana Cay, arguing that its dimensions and surrounding marine channels align more precisely with logbook sailing vectors.

perspectives.holder: Early Spanish chroniclers and traditional historiography (high demographic estimates, e.g. Library of Congress)
perspectives.account: Early Spanish reports and colonial accounts estimated the pre-contact Indigenous population of Hispaniola at roughly one million people, asserting that forced labor and disease reduced the population to thirty thousand within two decades.

perspectives.holder: Fernandes et al. (2021), Nature / Reich Laboratory (paleogenomic modeling)
perspectives.account: Genome-wide analyses of ancient Caribbean individuals indicate an effective population size of 1,530–8,150 across Hispaniola and Puerto Rico, demonstrating that pre-contact census sizes were substantially smaller than colonial estimates of hundreds of thousands to millions, while confirming catastrophic post-contact population collapse.

audience_note: This record documents colonial violence, the kidnapping and forced subjugation of Indigenous peoples, and the catastrophic demographic collapse of the Taíno population of the Caribbean resulting from Spanish encomienda forced labor, warfare, and introduced epidemic diseases.

importance.justification: The transatlantic voyage linked the Eastern and Western Hemispheres in permanent contact, inaugurating European colonization of the Americas, the transatlantic slave trade, and catastrophic Indigenous population collapse.

reviewer_note: Least sure of the exact island of Guanahaní (San Salvador vs Samana Cay) and pre-contact demographic baselines (colonial estimates of one million vs genomic Ne of 1,530–8,150).
